title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
author: Rebecca Skloot
target_audience: General readers interested in science and history
Students of bioethics, history of medicine, and African American studies
Readers interested in social justice and civil rights
core_themes: The intersection of race, class, and medicine in America
Scientific discovery and its human cost
primary_purpose: To reveal the untold story of Henrietta Lacks, whose cells became one of the most important tools in medicine, and to illuminate the complicated relationship between scientific progress, ethics, and the personal lives affected by research.

structure_format.narrative_style: Narrative nonfiction, blending personal memoir, history, and investigative reporting
structure_format.organization: Chronological interweaving of Henrietta’s life, her family’s experiences, and the scientific advancements enabled by HeLa cells
features: Interviews with family, scientists, and historians

key_concepts_lessons: Henrietta Lacks’s cells (HeLa cells) became the first immortal human cell line and revolutionized biomedical research.
Henrietta and her family were unaware of the use and impact of her cells, raising questions about consent and patient rights.
Systemic racism and socioeconomic inequality shaped the Lacks family’s experiences with healthcare and scientific institutions.
Medical progress can carry personal and ethical costs for individuals whose contributions are unacknowledged.
Recognition and respect for patients and research subjects are central to ethical medical practice.
notable_features: Blends science writing with personal storytelling
Examines both scientific advances and their ethical implications
Centers voices of Henrietta’s family, especially her daughter Deborah
Accessibility to general readers while remaining rigorous
cultural_historical_context: Published in 2010 amid renewed discussions about informed consent and bioethics, the book sheds light on unchecked medical practices prevalent in the mid-20th century, especially regarding African American patients in the segregated South.
reception_impact: Bestseller and influential in popular culture and academia
Sparked debate about bioethics, informed consent, and race in medicine
Praised for humanizing a scientific story and amplifying marginalized voices
comparable_titles: Medical Apartheid by Harriet A. Washington
The Emperor of All Maladies by Siddhartha Mukherjee
